original-en.context: ANTIGONE. Long-suffering father, Oedipus, the towers That fence the city still are faint and far; But where we stand is surely holy ground; A wilderness of laurel, olive, vine; Within a choir or songster nightingales Are warbling. On this native seat of rock Rest; for an old man thou hast traveled far.

modern-en.context: ANTIGONE. My long-suffering father, Oedipus — the towers that guard the city are still faint and far away. But the ground where we stand is surely holy: a wilderness of laurel, olive, and vine, and inside it a chorus of nightingales is singing. Rest here on this native seat of rock; for an old man, you have traveled far.

original-en.context: OEDIPUS. Child of an old blind sire, Antigone, What region, say, whose city have we reached? Who will provide today with scanted dole This wanderer? ’Tis little that he craves, And less obtains—that less enough for me; For I am taught by suffering to endure, And the long years that have grown old with me, And last not least, by true nobility. My daughter, if thou seest a resting place On common ground or by some sacred grove, Stay me and set me down. Let us discover Where we have come, for strangers must inquire Of denizens, and do as they are bid.

modern-en.context: OEDIPUS. Antigone, child of an old blind father — tell me, what country is this? Whose city have we reached? Who today will offer even a meager handout to this wanderer? He asks for little, and gets less — but that little is enough for me. Suffering has taught me to endure, and so have the long years that have grown old alongside me, and not least my own true nobility. My daughter, if you see any resting place on common ground or beside some sacred grove, stop me and set me down. Let us find out where we have come; strangers must ask those who live here, and do whatever they are told.

original-en.context: ANTIGONE. I see a woman Riding upon a colt of Aetna’s breed; She wears for headgear a Thessalian hat To shade her from the sun. Who can it be? She or a stranger? Do I wake or dream? ’Tis she; ’tis not—I cannot tell, alack; It is no other! Now her bright’ning glance Greets me with recognition, yes, ’tis she, Herself, Ismene!

original-en.context: ISMENE. The toil and trouble, father, that I bore To find thy lodging-place and how thou faredst, I spare thee; surely ’twere a double pain To suffer, first in act and then in telling; ’Tis the misfortune of thine ill-starred sons I come to tell thee. At the first they willed To leave the throne to Creon, minded well Thus to remove the inveterate curse of old, A canker that infected all thy race. But now some god and an infatuate soul Have stirred betwixt them a mad rivalry To grasp at sovereignty and kingly power. Today the hot-branded youth, the younger born, Is keeping Polyneices from the throne, His elder, and has thrust him from the land. The banished brother (so all Thebes reports) Fled to the vale of Argos, and by help Of new alliance there and friends in arms, Swears he will stablish Argos straight as lord Of the Cadmeian land, or, if he fail, Exalt the victor to the stars of heaven. This is no empty tale, but deadly truth, My father; and how long thy agony, Ere the gods pity thee, I cannot tell.

modern-en.context: ISMENE. The trouble and toil I took, father, to find where you were living and how you were faring — I spare you. It would be a double pain to live through and then to tell. I come to tell you about the misfortune of your ill-starred sons. At first they were willing to leave the throne to Creon, meaning to clear away the old, ingrained curse — the canker that had infected all your race. But now some god, and their own crazed minds, have stirred up a mad rivalry between them to grab at sovereignty and royal power. Today the hot-headed one, the younger son, is keeping Polyneices from the throne, his elder, and has driven him out of the land. The banished brother, so all Thebes reports, has fled to the vale of Argos. There, through new alliances and friends in arms, he swears he will either establish Argos as lord of the Cadmeian land, or — failing that — raise whoever beats him to the stars of heaven. This is no empty rumor, father, but deadly truth. How long your agony will continue before the gods pity you, I cannot say.
